questions.question: In a navigation framework you are building, what should each back stack entry own?
options: Only its route string; all screen state lives in one global app-wide object
Its destination and arguments, plus its lifecycle, ViewModels and saved state
A reference to the previous entry's composable, so it can be redrawn on Back
A snapshot copy of the whole back stack, taken at the moment the entry was pushed
questions.explanation: Each entry is a little host: it knows what to show, with which arguments, and owns lifecycle, ViewModels and saved state for that screen. That is what lets a screen under the top keep its state and be cleaned up properly when popped. A single global state object makes popping and restoring screens leak or lose data.

questions.question: The app is killed in the background and later restored. What must your navigation framework have saved to put the user back where they were?
options: The stack as destinations with arguments, plus each entry's saved state
Nothing at all; the system restores the Compose tree and its state automatically
Only the top entry, because the rest can be rebuilt from the start destination
Every entry's ViewModel instance, serialized into the Activity's saved state
questions.explanation: After process death only the saved state Bundle survives, so the framework must write the stack (routes and arguments) and each entry's saved state, then rebuild entries from it. Saving only the top makes Back go to the wrong place. ViewModel instances are not serializable; they are recreated and read what they need from SavedStateHandle.

questions.question: Why move from string routes like `"detail/$id"` to serializable route classes like `Detail(id: Long)`?
options: The compiler checks argument names and types instead of failing at runtime
Route classes navigate faster, because no string parsing has to happen
Route classes never need to be saved and restored across process death
String routes cannot carry more than one argument through to the destination
questions.explanation: With string routes, a typo in a key or a wrong type is only found when the screen fails to parse its arguments at runtime. A route class makes the destination's contract a compile-time type. It still has to be serialized into saved state, and performance is not the point.

questions.question: Passing large objects, such as a full list of items, as navigation arguments is fine because arguments only live in memory.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Arguments are stored in the entry's saved state, which goes into a Bundle that can exceed binder limits and fail with TransactionTooLargeException. Pass an ID and load the data from a repository in the destination.

questions.question: A notification deep link opens a product detail screen directly. What should Back do, and what must the framework support for it?
options: Exit the app, since the user arrived from outside it through the notification
Return to whatever screen the user visited last in their previous session
Show an empty placeholder screen while the start destination finishes loading
Go up the hierarchy, so the framework builds a synthetic stack like Home > Detail
questions.explanation: Users expect Back from a deep-linked screen to stay in the app and move up the hierarchy. The framework does this by building the parent entries when it handles the link. Restoring an old session is unpredictable and may not even match the linked content.

questions.question: When should a popped entry's ViewModelStore be cleared?
options: Immediately when `pop()` is called, before any animation starts
Never; keep it in case the user navigates forward again
After its exit transition finishes and it has left composition
When the Activity is destroyed, along with every other entry
questions.explanation: The outgoing screen is still on screen during its exit animation or a predictive back gesture, so clearing its ViewModels immediately can crash or blank it mid-animation. Clearing once it has really left composition avoids that. Keeping stores forever or until the Activity dies leaks every screen the user ever visited.

questions.question: A double tap on a button pushes the same screen twice. Which are correct ways to prevent this? Select all that apply.
options: Call `navigate()` directly in the composable body so it runs during composition
Skip pushing when the destination is already on top (single-top behavior)
Ignore navigate requests from an entry that is not in the RESUMED state
Store the navigation event in a StateFlow and replay it after rotation
questions.explanation: Single-top checks stop the same destination stacking on itself, and once the first tap starts a transition the source entry is no longer RESUMED, so a second tap can be ignored. Navigating during composition fires again on every recomposition. Replaying an event after rotation navigates twice, which is the opposite of what we want.

questions.question: A bottom bar has three tabs, and each tab should remember its own history when the user switches away and back. What does the framework need?
options: One shared back stack, cleared whenever the user taps a different tab
Save each tab's stack and state on leaving, and restore it on return
A separate Activity for each tab, so the system keeps each stack itself
Turn off state saving for tab screens to keep memory usage as low as possible
questions.explanation: Multiple back stacks means saving a tab's entries and their state when switching away and restoring them on return, often by popping to the tab root with save and restore flags. Clearing the stack loses the user's place. Separate Activities make shared UI and transitions much harder.

questions.question: In a single-Activity Compose app, the navigation framework should handle system Back by popping its own stack, and let the Activity handle it only when the stack has a single entry.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. The framework registers a back callback that is enabled only while it has something to pop. When only the start destination remains, it disables itself so the system can finish or background the Activity.

questions.question: Which behaviors does your framework need to support Android's predictive back gesture? Select all that apply.
options: Pop the entry as soon as the gesture starts, then push it back if cancelled
Keep the previous entry composed and visible while the gesture is in progress
Discard the previous entry's saved state while the gesture is in progress
Commit the pop only when the gesture completes, and restore the current screen if it is cancelled
questions.explanation: Predictive back shows the destination underneath while the user drags, driven by gesture progress, and the user can still cancel. So the framework previews the pop and only commits it at the end. Popping at the start destroys the current entry's state, and discarding the previous entry's state breaks the screen the user is about to see.
